abstract.p: Despite the success of vaccination and small-molecule antivirals in significantly reducing mortality from acute viral infections, chronic viral infections such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) remain persistent global health burdens. Latent reservoirs, drug resistance mutations, and immune evasion mechanisms enable these viruses to persist, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic approaches. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is an emerging immunotherapeutic strategy, initially developed to treat cancer, that harnesses a patient’s own immune cells to induce targeted immune responses. Chronic viral infections share significant similarities with tumors, including immune cell exhaustion, expression of inhibitory ligands, and metabolic suppression. Consequently, CAR-T-cell therapy holds promise as a new approach to treating chronic viral infections and has attracted considerable attention in recent years. This review systematically evaluates the progress in using CAR-T-cell therapy to treat chronic infections caused by HIV, HBV, CMV, and EBV, focusing on target selection and CAR-T-cell design strategies and highlighting the potential of these approaches to achieve disease control.

sec.p: Keywords: Virus diseases, Immunotherapy, Adoptive, Chimeric antigen

abstract.title: Highlighted points
abstract.p: CAR-T-cell therapy has shown progress against chronic viral infections, including HIV, HBV, CMV, and EBV. Constructs targeting multiple viral antigens have demonstrated antiviral activity in vitro and in animal models, and some have progressed to clinical trials. Despite these advances, CAR-T-cell therapy for chronic viral infections still faces key challenges, including the eradication of reservoirs, viral escape through mutations, risks of multiorgan toxicity, and ethical or regulatory concerns.

Future directions include optimizing the CAR design, creating multifunctional CAR-T cells, combining CAR-T cells with other immunotherapies, and deriving CAR-T cells from hematopoietic stem cells to increase persistence. In parallel, robust ethical oversight and regulatory frameworks will be essential to ensure safe and responsible clinical translation.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The human immune system defends against infection by limiting pathogen replication, reducing tissue damage, and forming immunological memory [1]. However, many viruses have evolved multiple mechanisms to evade immunity. With the exception of hepatitis C virus (HCV), no curative therapies have been developed for chronic viral infections—particularly HIV, HBV, CMV, and EBV—which, as a result, continue to represent long-term global public health burdens [2–4].

For example, more than 39 million people living with HIV must remain on lifelong, highly active antiretroviral therapy but still face the threat of latent proviral rebound [5]. Similarly, more than 296 million people worldwide live with chronic HBV infection, and they often experience viral flare-ups after discontinuing nucleotide analogs (NAs) because of residual covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) in their hepatocytes [6]; CMV and EBV have established latent infections in the majority of the global population and currently lack curative treatments [4]. Moreover, in organ transplant recipients, the reactivation of CMV or EBV is difficult to manage effectively with current antivirals owing to drug resistance and organ toxicity [7, 8]. In this context, novel approaches are highly anticipated.

Over the past three decades, clinical successes have established chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) as the “fourth pillar” of cancer treatment, following surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy [5]. Its fundamental goal is to genetically modify and expand T cells ex vivo and then reinfuse them to reconstitute anti-disease effector functions to overcome the T-cell exhaustion caused by persistent antigen stimulation. Chronic viral infections also exhibit molecular features analogous to those observed in tumors, thereby underscoring the potential applicability of CAR-T-cell therapy. In these patients, virus-specific T cells display sustained expression of inhibitory receptors—including PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3—leading to functional impairment [9]. Moreover, viral envelope proteins are stably expressed on the membranes of infected cells or virions, providing suitable and accessible targets for CAR-T recognition [10]. Lastly, the immune evasion strategy of MHC-I downregulation, which is typically adopted by chronic viruses, paradoxically benefits CAR-T cells, as their antigen recognition is MHC independent [11–13].

Therefore, the “exhaustion reversal–functional restoration” strategy validated in cancer treatment could theoretically be applied directly to chronic viral infections, providing a rationale for CAR-T-cell therapy in this context. sec.p: Existing CAR-T reviews rarely provide integrated comparisons of design strategies across different chronic viral infections. Many either span viruses, fungi, and tumors broadly but lack depth or focus exclusively on a single virus while sacrificing breadth. In contrast, this review systematically synthesizes CAR-T-cell research across multiple chronic viral infections. It addresses challenges common to CAR-T-cell therapy and highlights those unique to chronic viral infections, such as the potentially increased risk of ICANS and the susceptibility of CAR-T cells themselves to HIV infection. In addition, this review offers a comprehensive summary of future directions for improvement, extending beyond any single virus, with the aim of providing insights that may inform and inspire researchers working across diverse domains of chronic viral infections.

sec.title: Main text
sec.p: Chronic viral infections counteract the host immune system through multiple mechanisms—including immune evasion, antigenic heterogeneity, and viral latency reservoirs—which impair the function of virus-specific lymphocytes [12–14]. In contrast, CAR-T cells can partially overcome these barriers, and therefore they hold therapeutic promise.

Immune evasion is a key reason for the chronicity of viral infections. Viruses employ multiple strategies, including downregulation of MHC-I expression to impair CTL recognition, rapid antigenic drift to escape antibody and T-cell responses, and upregulation of the inhibitory molecules that drive T-cell exhaustion [15–17]. CAR-T cells can overcome some of these challenges through decreased levels of exhaustion, MHC-independent recognition, engineered CARS to target conserved viral epitopes, and the development of bispecific CARs to broaden antigen coverage [18–20]. Nevertheless, immune evasion may also interfere with CAR-T efficacy. For example, when the antigen targeted by CAR-T cells undergoes major mutations, CAR recognition is lost, resulting in therapeutic failure.

“Antigenic heterogeneity” refers to the variation in target antigen expression among different infected cells, enabling subsets to evade recognition through low antigen expression or mutational changes [21]. It also affects CAR-T-cell therapy. When the antigen density is low it may fall below the CAR activation threshold, preventing effective activation, expansion, or persistence [22]. Thus, CAR design often aims to achieve an optimal level of affinity to prevent evasion.
Viral latency reservoirs represent another key driver of chronic infection, with their role being particularly pronounced in HIV. A detailed discussion will be provided in the HIV section.

In summary, CAR-T cells can target several key mechanisms underlying the chronicity of viral infections, thereby displaying therapeutic potential. Compared with conventional antiviral therapies, CAR-T treatment may provide superior clinical benefits, as summarized in Table 1. In the following sections, we discuss the research progress of CAR-T-cell therapy involving different viruses Table 2, and then discuss common challenges and future perspectives.

sec.title: CAR-T-Cell therapy for HIV infection
sec.p: As of 2024, approximately 39 million people globally are infected with HIV, which has cumulatively caused over 40 million deaths. HIV infection remains a major global public health challenge [23]. Although long-term combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) can effectively suppress HIV replication, the latent reservoir prevents cure and causes rapid rebound after treatment interruption [8, 24]. Furthermore, continuous viral mutation drives resistance, limiting therapeutic options [25]. Therefore, new therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to eliminate or durably control the latent reservoir and overcome HIV’s resistance mutations to achieve drug-free sustained remission.

CAR-T therapy has the potential to recognize and eliminate HIV-infected cells specifically [8]. Unlike conventional drugs, CAR-T cells may persist in vivo for the long term, actively surveilling and destroying latently infected cells, thereby addressing the inability of cART to target the latent reservoir [26]. Moreover, CAR-T cells can be engineered to target resistant variants, thereby overcoming drug resistance. CAR-T-cell therapy may particularly benefit patients with drug-resistant or multi-strain infections. Consequently, CAR-T-cell therapy for HIV has attracted significant research attention in recent years.

sec.title: Key target designs for HIV-CAR-T cells
Early CAR design: CD4-based CARs
sec.p: Since the 1990s, researchers have attempted to use the HIV receptor CD4 as the recognition domain for CARs. By fusing the extracellular portion of the native CD4 receptor (domains 1 and 2) with T-cell activation signaling domains (e.g., the CD3ζ chain), CD4ζ CAR-T cells were constructed [18]. This design mediates direct binding to Env (gp120) on infected cells and cytotoxicity against Env-expressing targets.

In vitro studies demonstrated that CD4-CAR-T cells exhibit broad cytotoxic activity against target cells infected with diverse HIV strains. However, surface CD4+ T cells render CAR-T cells susceptible to HIV, causing functional loss/exhaustion [26].

Early trials revealed acceptable safety but limited efficacy: poor expansion/persistence and minimal or transient viral load reduction [7, 25]. These limitations were likely due to the infection of CAR-T cells by the virus and the short lifespan of the cells resulting from the lack of costimulatory signals.

sec.title: Second-generation CARs with costimulatory domains
sec.p: To address the short lifespan issue, researchers added T-cell costimulatory signaling domains (e.g., CD28 or 4-1BB) to the CD4-CAR backbone, resulting in the generation of second-generation anti-HIV CAR-T cells. This modification improved the T-cell expansion capacity and resistance to exhaustion [25, 27, 28].

Clinical trials of second-generation anti-HIV CAR-T cells have shown improved persistence and a partial reduction in HIV DNA and reservoir cells [25]. However, single infusions failed to achieve durable control, with epitope mutations observed [6]. Although a functional cure was not achieved, the study offered valuable insights. These findings indicated that, when constrained by reservoir protection and viral escape, CAR-T cells targeting a single epitope struggle to control the virus fully.

sec.title: Bispecific or multispecific CAR-T cells
sec.p: To reduce opportunities for viral escape, researchers have developed bispecific CARs. This strategy can be implemented either by incorporating two recognition domains into a single CAR molecule or by co-expressing two distinct CARs on the same T cell. By recognizing distinct antigens, bispecific CARs can prevent target cells from escaping through the downregulation of a single antigen [20]. Their dual binding also enhances the efficiency of CAR signaling and stabilizes engagement with target cells, thereby improving CAR-T-cell activation and cytotoxicity. However, the more complex structure may compromise expression stability and introduce challenges in vector design, packaging, and large-scale manufacturing [29].

Li Liu et al. developed a “CD4-17b” bispecific CAR that contains the CD4 extracellular domains and the single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of the human 17b monoclonal antibody, which recognizes a highly conserved epitope on gp120. This bispecific CAR showed stronger cytotoxicity and resistance to HIV-1 infection [30].

To refine this approach, researchers omitted the CD4 and instead combined two anti-Env scFvs within one CAR molecule, creating bispecific CAR-T cells termed “duoCAR-T cells”. This design reduced HIV infection by > 97% in vitro and in vivo and remained effective against resistant strains. Critically, duoCAR-T cells resisted HIV-1 infection, suggesting their potential for long-term viral control [31–33]. A phase I/IIa clinical trial of duoCAR-T cells involving 18 participants is currently ongoing and is expected to be completed in 2028 [32].

These studies indicate that bispecific CAR-T cells unexpectedly avoid being infected by the virus themselves in vitro. The likely avoidance mechanism involves multiple anti-HIV binding domains on the CAR-T cells simultaneously binding to different conserved sites on the HIV envelope glycoprotein, thereby preventing the virus from entering the CAR-T cells. However, these studies also have limitations: CAR-T cells remain ineffective against the viral reservoir sequestered on follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) [34].

Another bispecific design strategy involves fusing recognition domains for CD4 and gp120 high-mannose glycans. This bispecific CAR binds both protein epitopes on Env and conserved high-mannose residues on the envelope, enabling more comprehensive targeting of the “native” viral envelope structure. This approach enhances potency without off-target recognition of host self-antigens [35]. Among the different high-mannose glycan targets, the potency of CD4-MBL and CD4-Langerin CAR-T cells was superior to that of CD4 CAR-T cells against all genetically diverse HIV-1 isolates [35]. In rhesus macaques, CD4-MBL CAR-T cells persisted for < 28 days because of antibodies against the CD4 domain. This finding highlights the importance of using CARs with lower immunogenicity (e.g., CARs targeting MBL or other gp120 high-mannose glycans) to extend CAR-T-cell survival in vivo [36]. Agnes Hajduczki et al. further developed a trispecific CAR, the CD4-MBL-R5Nt CAR, by adding the C–C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5) N-terminal region to the CD4-MBL CAR. Compared with CD4-MBL CAR-T cells, this construct showed enhanced anti-HIV activity in vitro [37].

Recent progress has been made with bispecific CAR-T cells targeting HIV and other diseases. For example, CAR-T cells directed against both CD19 and HIV gp120 have demonstrated the ability to kill tumor cells and control viral infection in vitro, suggesting potential applications for patients with concomitant lymphoma and HIV [38]. In addition, the number of CMV-specific HIV-CAR-T cells has advanced substantially over the past two years, and these cells have already entered clinical trials, which will be elaborated upon in the subsequent section on CMV bispecific CAR-T strategies [39].

In summary, although CAR-T cells with double CARs have an improved ability to kill HIV-infected cells and HIV infection can be blocked by CAR-T cells in vitro, refining the CAR alone is insufficient to eradicate the latent HIV reservoir. Crucially, it does not fundamentally resolve the intrinsic susceptibility of CD4+ CAR-T cells to HIV infection. Therefore, broader innovations in CAR-T-cell design are being pursued.

sec.title: Innovations in overall HIV CAR-T-cell design
HIV CAR-T cells targeting the viral reservoir
sec.p: Most HIV replication occurs within secondary lymphoid organs (SLOs), such as the spleen, lymph nodes, and gut-associated lymphoid tissue. In chronic, untreated infection, HIV RNA+ cells are concentrated in B-cell follicles, such as germinal centers within SLOs, where they evade cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) killing through multiple mechanisms, including the following [40]:

list-item.p: Lack of follicular homing receptors: CTLs do not express the C–X–C chemokine receptor type 5 (CXCR5) receptor required for homing to B-cell follicles, preventing their effective entry into these follicular regions;
Local T-cell exhaustion: CD8+ T cells within follicles display an exhausted phenotype with impaired cytotoxic function;

Integration and Epigenetic Silencing: Many viruses, including retroviruses such as HIV and herpesviruses such as EBV and CMV, integrate into host chromosomes or persist episomally in the nucleus. Epigenetic silencing suppresses viral gene expression, making infected cells immunologically “invisible” [41].

Lack of follicular homing receptors: CTLs do not express the C–X–C chemokine receptor type 5 (CXCR5) receptor required for homing to B-cell follicles, preventing their effective entry into these follicular regions;

Low Antigen Expression and Immune Evasion: Latent infection is characterized by very low or intermittent antigen expression, accompanied by multiple immune evasion mechanisms that limit immune recognition.

sec.p: CAR-T cells can overcome these mechanisms to some extent. Engineered CAR-T cells can be modified to traffic into the viral reservoir. As noted above, compared with patients’ HIV-specific T cells, CAR-T cells exhibit less exhaustion and superior functionality. Although latent cells usually do not produce viral proteins, some latency-associated proteins can still serve as potential CAR-T-cell targets.

Despite the many advantages of CAR-T-cell therapy, latent reservoirs remain the central barrier limiting its efficacy. A subset of latently infected cells expresses few surface antigens, making them difficult for CAR-T cells to recognize and eliminate [14]. In parallel, viral escape through Env epitope mutation and antigenic heterogeneity can reduce CAR recognition affinity and activation thresholds, thereby enabling rapid evasion of CAR-T-cell activity [42]. Although clinical trials have shown that CAR-T-cell therapy can significantly reduce the levels of cell-associated viral RNA and intact proviruses, all the participants who underwent ART interruption ultimately experienced viral rebound. Importantly, rebound viruses frequently harbor variants that are partially resistant to CAR-T-mediated cytotoxicity [6]. These observations suggest that both latent reservoirs and viral escape act in concert to limit the long-term efficacy of CAR-T-cell therapy. The following are potential strategies to address this challenge.

sec.title: CXCR5-coexpressing HIV CAR-T for follicular reservoir access
sec.p: SIV-CAR-T cells with CXCR5 suppressed SIV replication in vitro and demonstrated CXCL13-directed migration and follicular homing ex vivo [43]. These findings demonstrate that equipping CAR-T cells with a follicular homing receptor enables them to access follicles and reach the HIV reservoir.

Clinical trials combining bispecific CARs with CXCR5 are already underway. M10 CAR-T cells are a novel multifunctional HIV-CAR-T-cell product with the chemokine receptor CXCR5 and a bispecific CAR. In a phase I study of 18 patients, M10 CAR-T cells controlled plasma viral loads in 74.3% of infusion cycles and reduced cell-associated HIV-1 RNA in 10 patients during 150 days of follow-up [25]. This is one of the most compelling early clinical studies supporting the application of CAR-T-cell therapy to HIV.
In summary, the incorporation of CXCR5 promotes follicular homing and reservoir clearance, representing a promising avenue toward a functional HIV cure.

sec.title: Anti-PD-1 HIV CAR-T cells
sec.p: To counteract the immunosuppressive microenvironment of HIV reservoirs and prevent rapid CAR-T-cell exhaustion, Karsten Eichholz et al. designed an anti-PD-1 CAR-T-cell without detectable cell-surface PD-1. In rhesus macaques, anti-PD-1 CAR-T cells cleared HIV reservoir cells, including germinal center (GC) TFH cells, and eradicated SIV from this immune sanctuary [44]. These findings indicate that CAR-T cells equipped with resistance to exhaustion can effectively exert cytotoxic functions within HIV reservoir sites, potentially clearing viruses and offering a strategy for HIV cure.

sec.title: HIV-Resistant CAR-T Engineering
sec.p: CD4+ CAR-T cells are inherently vulnerable to HIV infection. Although bispecific CAR-T cells can block viral entry and thereby protect themselves from HIV, whether this protection holds in vivo within high-HIV-concentration viral reservoirs remains uncertain. Therefore, researchers are exploring additional ways to protect CAR-T cells, especially CD4+ CAR-T cells, from HIV infection.

One advanced strategy is site-specific CAR integration into the CCR5 locus, disrupting this major HIV co-receptor and conferring resistance to R5-tropic strains [45–47]. Using a clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/Cas9 (CRISPR/Cas9) genome editing system, researchers inserted a CAR derived from the broadly neutralizing antibody 10–1074 into the CCR5 locus. The resulting CAR-T cells specifically killed HIV-infected cells both in vitro and in humanized mouse models while resisting infection [45, 48]. In addition to CRISPR/Cas9, homology-directed recombination (HDR)-mediated insertion into CCR5 similarly yielded CCR5-negative CAR-T cells that were resistant to HIV-1 infection [49, 50]. The expression of dual anti-HIV-1 shRNAs in CAR-T cells also conferred resistance to infection [51].

Different technical approaches can achieve CAR integration at the CCR5 locus, mechanistically reducing HIV infection of CAR-T cells and extending their persistence [46]. Furthermore, co-expressing a fusion inhibitor peptide (C34–CXCR4) in CAR-T cells can similarly block HIV from infecting CAR-T cells [27].

In summary, there are multiple strategies to prevent HIV infection of CAR-T cells, providing a strong guarantee for the long-term persistence of the cells. This research represents a significant step forward toward a “curative gene therapy” approach to HIV.

sec.title: synNotch receptor-engineered bifunctional CAR-T cells
sec.p: In recent years, a novel bifunctional CAR-T strategy based on the synNotch receptor was proposed for cancer and subsequently introduced into HIV therapy [52, 53]. When both the synNotch receptor and the CAR simultaneously recognize their respective antigens, CAR-T cells can be activated, preventing the chronic activation and exhaustion. Additionally, these CAR-T cells not only secrete the broadly neutralizing antibody VRC01 to neutralize free virus but also release a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) (N6-αCD3) to bridge bystander T cells to infected cells [54]. In the future, the synNotch system may be applied to various chronic viral infections to optimize the long-term efficacy of CAR-T-cell therapy.

sec.title: Broadly neutralizing antibody-derived CARs
sec.p: Most HIV-specific CAR-T cells discussed above are based on the CD4 receptor, which makes T cells susceptible to HIV infection and imposes specific selective pressure that promotes viral escape. Therefore, the development of new targeting domains is imperative.

With the discovery of numerous bNAbs, researchers have begun using neutralizing antibody fragments against HIV as the CAR recognition domain. This approach provides a diverse array of targets with high affinity, improving coverage across multiple HIV strains. Prominent examples include CARs constructed using scFvs derived from bNAbs such as VRC01, 3BNC117, and 10–1074 [55]. The resulting CAR-T cells exhibit enhanced recognition capabilities and potent, specific killing of HIV-infected T cells [55].

sec.title: Clinical trials
sec.p: Early first-generation CD4ζ CAR-T trials in humans have confirmed the feasibility, tolerability, and persistence of these cells, but their antiviral effects are limited [56–59]. Since 2020, Env-targeted, bNAb-derived, and multifunctional CAR designs have shown improved biological activity and safety, with evidence of reservoir reduction and selective pressure on rebound viruses, although their depth and breadth remain insufficient [6, 25].

Current HIV-CAR-T-cell clinical trials have evolved from single-target constructs to multi-target and functionally enhanced designs, with multiple phase I/I–II studies ongoing or registered (e.g., NCT04648046, NCT06252402, NCT03240328, NCT04863066, NCT03617198, and NCT06880380) [60–65]. Most strategies employ bispecific or multifunctional CARs to increase antigen coverage (e.g., LVgp120 duoCAR), as complemented by enhancements such as CMV-specific CAR-T-cell backbones, neutralizing antibody-derived CARs, and follicular homing modifications. Key challenges include in vivo expansion and persistence, recognition of low-antigen or latent cells, and resistance to viral escape. If successful, these trials will provide the first clinical validation of a functional cure strategy for HIV and serve as a model for CAR-T-cell translational strategies in the broader field of chronic viral infections.

sec.title: CAR-T-Cell therapy for HBV infection
sec.p: In addition to HIV, HBV infection is also a major global public health challenge, with an estimated 296 million people chronically infected and nearly 1 million HBV-related deaths annually [66]. Existing antivirals such as nucleotide analogs effectively suppress HBV replication but have minimal effects on the cccDNA reservoir in hepatocytes, allowing the virus to rebound once treatment is stopped [66, 67]

Moreover, chronic HBV carriers in immunosuppressed states—such as those taking immunosuppressants, undergoing chemotherapy, or being post-organ transplant—can experience HBV reactivation that severely worsens outcomes [16, 68–71]. In addition, standard prophylactic antiviral therapy may fail to prevent HBV reactivation; for instance, HBV reactivation has occurred after CAR-T-cell therapy despite entecavir prophylaxis [72–74]. HBV co-infection is also not uncommon in immunodeficient individuals, such as people living with HIV, whose prevalence is significantly higher than that in healthy individuals [75–77]. Even under HBV treatment, occult HBV replication (that is undetectable by classical methods) remains relatively common in HIV/HBV-co-infected patients [78].

Therefore, therapeutic approaches beyond standard antivirals are urgently needed for chronic HBV infection, and CAR-T-cell therapy is a promising option. Younger patients who wish to avoid lifelong antiviral therapy and actively seek a functional cure may benefit from it. Studies indicate that the HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) is present on the plasma membrane of HBV-infected cells, making them potential targets for CAR-T-cell attacks [79]. Current CAR-T development efforts for HBV have focused primarily on targeting the HBsAg, including epitopes in the small S region and the PreS1 region of the large envelope protein [80].

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting HBsAg
sec.p: Krebs et al. first demonstrated that HBsAg-specific CAR-T cells can recognize viral particles from multiple HBV subtypes [16] and that these cells exhibit antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo. However, the direct killing efficacy of CAR-T cells against HBV+ cell lines is relatively limited. This limitation may be due to low levels of HBsAg on infected cell surfaces or the predominantly soluble form of the antigen, suggesting that CAR design may need optimization for enhanced cytotoxicity. Furthermore, because the HBV genome can integrate into host cell DNA, CAR-T cells struggle to eliminate all virus-containing hepatocytes, resulting in functional control of HBV rather than complete elimination [81, 82].

Notably, in mouse models, HBsAg-CAR-T cells survived and proliferated even without prior host lymphodepletion. Improvements in virological markers were achieved with only transient, mild liver injury, and no uncontrolled cytokine storm was observed [16, 81]. These studies demonstrate a favorable safety profile for HBsAg-targeted CAR-T cells. Importantly, they suggest that CAR-T-cell persistence might not require deep lymphodepletion, potentially avoiding the increased risk of HBV reactivation associated with intensive conditioning regimens [82].

sec.title: Higher affinity CARs
sec.p: CAR affinity for its target directly affects CAR-T-cell killing efficacy. To develop CARs with higher affinity for HBsAg, Sophia Schreiber et al. isolated HBV-specific memory B cells from HBV-infected patients by single B cell sorting. They cloned two highly specific anti-HBsAg antibodies, 4D06 and 4D08, which showed broad reactivity and neutralizing capacity against all major HBV genotypes. CARs derived from these antibodies performed well, with robust cytokine secretion and killing of HBV-positive target cells [83].
This study provides an efficient and rapid method for identifying human monoclonal antibodies for new HBV CAR targets.

Mayank Srivastava et al. went a step further by developing a comprehensive strategy for CAR target discovery. They reconstructed patient-specific HBV genomes, identified human chromosomal regions containing integrated HBV sequences, and used a human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I immunoproteomics platform to survey the HBV peptide epitopes present on infected cells. This approach identified and validated novel HBV-derived, HLA-I–presented peptides that can guide the development of new CAR targets [84].
Researchers are clearly pursuing diverse methods of HBV CAR-T-cell screening to identify higher-affinity targets, paving the way for more effective HBV CAR-T-cell products in the future.

sec.title: Clinical trials
sec.p: To date, no CAR-T-cell therapies specifically targeting HBV have been reported in clinical trials, although HBV-specific T-cell receptor (TCR)-T-cell therapies have entered trials. This lack of CAR-T-cell clinical data is largely due to the inherent limitations of HBV-directed CAR-T-cell therapy:

The current HBV-CAR-T cells primarily recognize HBV envelope proteins such as HBsAg. However, these antigens typically circulate at extremely high concentrations in the serum of chronic HBV patients, creating an “antigen sink”. Soluble HBsAg binds to the CAR recognition domains on CAR-T cells, thereby “sequestering” them and preventing the effective recognition and killing of target cells. Moreover, this approach leads to overactivation and immune exhaustion [85]. Therefore, HBsAg-CAR-T cells exhibit suboptimal cytotoxic function at present and are difficult to advance to clinical trials [81].

Additionally, following viral integration into host cells, the HBV genome is often incomplete and rarely produces full-length surface antigens. Integrated DNA-derived peptides presented on MHC-I are too short to be recognized by HBsAg-specific CARs, leaving subsets of infected cells undetected [86]. The cccDNA in the hepatocyte nucleus is the central reservoir of HBV. Notably, cccDNA transcriptional activity is highly heterogeneous [87]. Cells with extremely low viral mRNA levels remain invisible to HBsAg-targeted CAR-T-cell clearance. These factors make complete eradication of HBV particularly challenging, and targeting hepatocytes with transcriptionally inactive cccDNA remains a critical area of research. At present, supporting durable in vivo persistence of CAR-T cells appears to be the best strategy for controlling HBV rebound.

These two major issues hinder the development of HBV CAR-T cells. Overcoming the antigen sink effect and expanding the range of targeted HBV-infected cells are critical challenges that must be addressed before CAR-T-cell therapy can be successful against chronic HBV infection.

sec.title: PreS1-targeted CAR-T: a possible route to eradicate chronic HBV
sec.p: To avoid the antigen sink, researchers have developed CAR-T cells that target the PreS1 region of the large HBV envelope protein [10]. PreS1 contains a viral receptor binding site for hepatocyte entry. It is relatively conserved and present only at low levels in soluble form, preventing the antigen sink effect and making it an attractive target [88].

Compared with traditional HBsAg-specific CAR-T cells, PreS1-specific CAR-T cells exhibit stronger in vitro killing activity against HBV-infected target cells [10]. Notably, the circulating HBsAg antigen did not lead to PreS1-specific CAR-T-cell inactivation or overactivation, demonstrating the absence of an “antigen sink” effect [16].

One of the strongest pieces of preclinical evidence to support the application of CAR-T-cell therapy in HBV infection is provided by PreS1- CAR-T cells. Guo et al. reported that after a single infusion of 2H5–A14 PreS1-CAR-T cells, multiple virological markers in serum and liver tissue (including HBsAg, HBV DNA, and cccDNA) in mouse models decreased below the detection limit [10]. These findings suggest that CAR-T cells nearly eradicated HBV infection in vivo. This study provides the first in vivo evidence that CAR-T cells targeting PreS1 have the potential to clear chronic HBV infection and achieve a functional cure [10]. However, this mouse model lacks a human immune system and does not fully recapitulate the immune environment of chronic HBV in patients. Therefore, the safety and efficacy of PreS1-targeted CAR-T-cell therapy require further validation in more complex models and, ultimately, in clinical trials.

sec.title: CAR-T cell therapy for CMV infection
sec.p: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a latent herpesvirus that poses minimal threat to immunocompetent individuals, but it has high incidence in and significant clinical impact on organ transplant recipients, patients who have received CAR-T-cell therapy, and other immunosuppressed individuals [89].

Studies have revealed that herpesviruses dominate early infections after CAR-T-cell therapy, with CMV reactivation being particularly prominent and associated with poor patient outcomes [90–94]. Furthermore, CMV reactivation can directly affect multiple organs, posing a widespread threat. Cases reported after various CAR-T-cell therapies include cytomegalovirus retinitis [95–97] cytomegalovirus colitis [98, 99], cytomegalovirus pneumonia [100, 101], and cytomegalovirus encephalitis [102].
Therefore, effectively preventing and treating CMV infection in immunocompromised patients remains a major challenge.

Traditional antiviral drugs are the first-line option but have significant limitations. First, antiviral resistance is not uncommon: approximately 5–12% of transplant patients develop ganciclovir-resistant CMV strains after treatment [103]. Second, common second-line drugs (such as foscarnet and cidofovir) have poor tolerability because of dose-limiting toxicity and severe side effects (e.g., renal impairment and myelosuppression) [103]. Lastly, conventional antivirals primarily inhibit viral replication and do not restore CMV-specific immune surveillance. Under conditions of profound immunosuppression (for example, using high-dose corticosteroids to treat CAR-T-related CRS), relying solely on antivirals may fail to control CMV reactivation.

These factors have driven the exploration of novel therapies. CAR-T-cell therapy, as one such approach, has gained significant attention. This therapy may be especially valuable for CMV carriers who are immunocompromised or who are receiving antitumor CAR-T-cell therapy.

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting cytomegalovirus glycoprotein B (gB)
sec.p: The first report on CAR-T cells engineered against CMV was published in 2010, when Full et al. designed a CAR targeting gB [104]. gB is a major structural protein expressed on infected cell surfaces during both the early and late phases of CMV replication. The gB-specific CAR-T cells in Full et al. were strongly activated upon co-culture with CMV-infected cells, resulting in significant degranulation and cytokine secretion. However, somewhat surprisingly, they were not very effective at inducing apoptosis or lysis of the infected cells and failed to clear CMV infection fully in vitro [104]. Subsequent studies confirmed this phenomenon: CMV-infected cells are resistant to gB CAR-T-cell-mediated killing [105, 106]. This resistance is closely linked to CMV-encoded anti-apoptotic factors. For example, viral proteins such as UL37 and UL36 interfere with mitochondrial and death-receptor apoptotic signaling pathways, respectively, directly blocking CAR-T-cell cytotoxicity and protecting infected host cells [105]. Although gB-CAR-T cells did not directly lyse infected cells, the high levels of cytokines they secreted inhibited viral replication in vitro. This non-cytolytic antiviral effect reduced the CMV load within infected cells to some extent [104, 107].

In 2021, Henning Olbrich et al. constructed novel gB-CAR-T cells using an scFv derived from the high-affinity gB-specific neutralizing monoclonal antibody SM5-1. This construct greatly increased the CAR’s affinity for CMV-infected cells, enabling effective recognition and lysis of HCMV-infected cells. In mouse models, these improved gB-CAR-T cells significantly reduced CMV infection [108], overcoming the limitations of early gB-CAR-T cells and making gB-CAR-T-cell application feasible. This is among the most convincing preclinical studies on the use of CAR-T cells for CMV infection.

sec.title: CARs targeting cytomegalovirus glycoprotein H (gH) and the UL128-131 complex
sec.p: To address the shortcomings of early gB-CAR-T cells, researchers have also sought alternative or complementary targets. In addition to gB, CMV has multiple other surface glycoproteins that can serve as targets for CAR’s derived from neutralizing antibodies.

In 2020, Ali et al. designed and constructed 8 different CARs targeting various epitopes using sequences from multiple anti-CMV neutralizing antibodies. These targets included the gH glycoprotein and the UL128-131 Complex. In CMV, gH and gL can form a pentameric complex with the UL128-131 Complex that is essential for entry into epithelial and endothelial cells, making both gH and the UL128–131A proteins compelling additional targets beyond gB. Among them, a CAR-T-cell line called 21E9-CAR-T (targeting an epitope on gH) showed the highest cytokine release levels and, importantly, effectively and stably lysed CMV-infected target cells [109].
This study demonstrated that by selecting appropriate viral surface antigen epitopes, CAR-T cells can gain the ability to clear CMV infection directly, offering a potential strategy for curing CMV.

sec.title: Innovative strategy: CAR design targeting CMV-FcRs
sec.p: In addition to targeting viral structural proteins directly, the immune-evasion molecules of CMV have become novel targets for CAR design. CMV encodes receptor-like proteins (the RL11 family of viral Fc receptors or CMV-FcRs) that bind the Fc region of host IgG. These viral FcR proteins are expressed on infected cell surfaces and act as antibody “decoys” to interfere with host antibody-mediated immunity [106].

Proff et al. leveraged this feature to design a unique CAR structure by using mutated IgG1/IgG4-derived CH2–CH3 regions as the hinge/spacer within the CAR molecule. These CAR-T cells can recognize and bind to CMV-FcRs on infected cell surfaces without interference from normal circulating IgG [106]. Studies have shown that CMV-infected cells begin highly expressing CMV-FcRs by approximately 3 days after infection, strongly activating gB-CAR-T cells containing the CH2–CH3 domain and enhancing CAR-T-cell effector function.

This ingenious design provides an alternative pathway for CAR-T cells to recognize CMV-infected cells: by targeting key molecules of the virus’ immune evasion machinery, it helps overcome CMV’s defenses [104].

sec.title: Bispecific CAR-T cells and clinical trials
sec.p: As mentioned, patients with hematological malignancies often experience CMV reactivation after CAR-T-cell therapy, which can worsen their prognosis. One preventive strategy is to construct CAR-T cells that target both the malignant cells and the CMV, thereby treating the cancer while simultaneously preventing CMV reactivation. This is CMV-specific CAR-T. Unlike conventional bispecific CAR-T, here, the CAR target is a tumor antigen, but the T-cell source is CMV-specific T cells.

Xiuli Wang et al. developed CMV-specific CD19-CAR-T cells with dual functions: treating B-cell lymphoma and preventing CMV reactivation [110]. Xiuli Wang et al. further reported that after stimulation with a CMV pp65 vaccine, CMV-specific CD19-CAR-T cells showed proliferative responses and enhanced anti-tumor activity in vitro [111]. These findings suggest that the anti-tumor effects of CMV-specific CD19-CAR-T cells not only prevent CMV reactivation but also are enhanced by subsequent CMV pp65 vaccination. This dual-benefit approach holds considerable clinical promise and is being clinically tested. Several recent phase I clinical trials (e.g., NCT05432635, NCT05801913, and NCT06735690) are evaluating CMV-specific CD19 CAR-T cells combined with the CMV vaccine, with the aim of assessing safety, dose escalation feasibility, and in vivo expansion potential [112–114].

In fact, as early as 2015, the clinical trial NCT01109095 investigated CMV-specific HER2-CAR-T cells. The results demonstrated preliminary safety and durable clinical benefit, providing the earliest evidence of the feasibility of CMV-specific CAR-T-cell therapy in humans [115].

Beyond CD19+ tumors, other therapeutic CAR-T cells can similarly be equipped to prevent viral reactivation. For example, Li Zhou et al. engineered virus-specific T cells (VSTs) to express a chimeric antigen receptor targeting the CD123 antigen on acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells. These CD123-CAR-VSTs could recognize epitopes from EBV, adenovirus, and CMV, and they demonstrated specific killing of CD123+ leukemia cell lines—showing potential for simultaneously treating AML and preventing multiple viral infections [116].

In addition to their oncology applications, bispecific CMV-specific CAR-T cells could also benefit people with HIV, in whom CMV co-infection is common and difficult to cure. In humanized HIV mouse models, similar to the behavior of CMV-specific CD19-CAR-T cells, CMV-specific HIV-CAR-T cells expanded robustly after CMV vaccination [39, 117]. This strategy could treat CMV while also improving HIV treatment efficacy, representing an attractive future direction. Testing of CMV-specific HIV-CAR-T cells in humans began in 2024 for the first time [61].

sec.title: CAR-T cell therapy for chronic active EBV infection (CAEBV)
sec.p: CAEBV is a highly fatal lymphoproliferative disorder caused by persistent EBV replication, with an approximately 50% five-year mortality rate [118]. Conventional antivirals and immunosuppressive therapies have very limited efficacy against CAEBV, and symptoms often recur. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), currently the only treatment capable of inducing long-term remission or cure, is limited by high transplant-related mortality and severe graft-versus-host disease [119].

CAR-T-cell therapy, a novel approach with potentially fewer complications, offers an opportunity to achieve a cure for CAEBV safely and presents an advantage for patients who are unwilling to undergo transplantation. CAEBV results from persistent EBV infection of T or NK cells. Commonly expressed viral antigens include latent membrane proteins (LMP) and envelope glycoproteins such as gp350, which serve as primary targets for CAR-T cells [120, 121]. CAEBV shares pathological similarities with EBV-positive lymphomas, with infected target cells expressing similar EBV-associated surface proteins. Therefore, the existing CAR-T-cell therapies targeting EBV antigens for EBV-positive lymphomas have paved the way for therapeutic CAR-T-cell therapy in CAEBV [122, 123].

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting LMP1
sec.p: The earliest constructed EBV-specific CAR-T cells targeted LMP1. LMP1-CAR-T cells demonstrated specific killing effects on LMP1-positive tumor cells and significantly reduced tumor volume in LMP1-high-expressing tumors in in vivo experiments [124, 125]. This work provides the first proof-of-concept that CAR-T-cell therapy could be effective in treating CAEBV, laying the foundation for subsequent CAR-T-cell strategies.

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting gp350
sec.p: gp350 is the primary mediator of the EBV’s entry into B cells, and it can be expressed on infected cell surfaces during viral reactivation. Recent reports have described CAR-T cells targeting gp350 [121].

gp350-CAR-T cells specifically recognized and eliminated EBV-infected tumor cell lines during in vitro co-culture. In animal models, it controlled the plasma EBV levels and inhibited the growth of EBV+ tumors [126–128]. These studies suggest that gp350-CAR-T cells can clear EBV-infected cells and could be used in attempts to cure CAEBV. However, one study reported that compared with CD19 CAR-T cells, gp350 CAR-T cells had inferior killing efficacy against EBV-infected Burkitt lymphoma cells in vivo, indicating that its clinical value requires further evaluation [129].

Clinical research on CAR-T cells for CAEBV is extremely limited. In the most recent case report, a 14-year-old CAEBV patient received gp350-CAR-T-cell therapy [130]. The patient showed significant clinical improvement following CAR-T-cell infusion, with sustained negativity for EBV DNA in their peripheral blood over 15 months of follow-up. Only Grade 1 CRS occurred during treatment, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of gp350-CAR-T cells in this case. This result represents one of the closest and most compelling pieces of evidence for the clinical application of CAR-T-cell therapy. Furthermore, CAR-T-cell clinical trials for EBV-positive lymphomas are ongoing. For example, an autologous gp350-targeted CAR-T-cell product (BRG01, NCT05864924) has entered the clinical stage, providing a reference for future clinical application in CAEBV.

In addition to traditional lentiviral CAR-T-cell manufacturing, virus-free methods are being explored, offering a safer manufacturing process [129, 131]. A recent study used a one-step CRISPR/Cas approach to insert an anti-EBV (gp350) CAR into T cells while simultaneously knocking out the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) [132]. These GRKO CAR-T cells exhibited specific cytotoxicity against gp350-expressing target cells and were insensitive to dexamethasone treatment. This observation provides a proof-of-concept for a virus-free method to manufacture glucocorticoid-resistant CAR-T-cell products. It also suggests that glucocorticoid-resistant gp350 CAR-T cells could be a future therapeutic option for high-risk post-transplant patients experiencing EBV reactivation or EBV-associated pathologies requiring steroid therapy.

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting LMP2A
sec.p: LMP2A expression is often detectable in CAEBV patients, whereas LMP1 expression levels are typically low [120, 121]. These findings suggest that LMP2A might be a more accessible target. However, research on LMP2A-CAR-T cells began later than that on LMP1-CAR-T cells did. To date, the first and only explicitly reported LMP2A-CAR-T cells were constructed in 2018 [133].

LMP2A-CAR-T cells are rare because LMP2A is a transmembrane protein whose extracellular region consists only of very short loops and lacks sufficient extracellular epitopes for direct CAR recognition [134]. In contrast, LMP1 possesses multiple extracellular domains, making it more suitable for CAR recognition.

sec.title: CAR-T cells targeting Epstein‒Barr Nuclear Antigen (EBNA)
sec.p: EBNA comprises a group of latent proteins expressed within the nucleus of EBV-infected cells. Full-length proteins are not detectable on the cell membrane, historically precluding their use as CAR-T-cell targets [135]. However, Anna Christina Dragon et al. developed a CAR based on the monoclonal antibody TU165. TU165-CAR-T cells recognized EBNA-3C-derived peptide/HLA complexes on the cell surface in a TCR-like manner, effectively targeting EBNA. They also created more potent TRUCK TU165-CAR-T cells, which additionally induced interleukin-12 release upon target engagement and subsequently recruited more immune cells. This research demonstrated a new and promising strategy to target the intracellular antigens of EBV-infected cells specifically, significantly expanding the range of potential CAR-T-cell targets [136].

sec.title: Bispecific CAR-T for EBV
sec.p: Like CMV, EBV bispecific CAR-T cells—also referred to as EBV-specific CAR-T cells—are constructed on the basis of EBV-specific T cells. Similarly, it aims not only to exert antitumor effects but also to prevent viral reactivation while leveraging viral antigens to enhance antitumor activity [137, 138]. Recently, several phase I/early-phase clinical trials have been initiated using EBV-specific CAR-T cells as platforms (e.g., NCT04288726, NCT04952584, and NCT06429800) [139–141]. These studies focus on assessing safety, dose-limiting toxicity, in vivo expansion capacity, and persistence, thereby providing preliminary evidence for the clinical feasibility of EBV-targeted CAR-T-cell therapy. Notably, NCT04952584 has been marked as Withdrawn (lack of funding), suggesting that lack of financial support was likely the primary reason for its termination. Moreover, NCT06429800 was also withdrawn, although the specific reason was not disclosed. Together, these cases highlight that EBV-specific CAR-T-cell clinical trials may face multiple opaque risks, including those related to funding, regulatory approval, or trial design.

sec.title: Clinical evidence of the effects of EBV-CAR-T cells
sec.p: In CAEBV- and EBV-associated tumors, infected and malignant cells both express EBV antigens. Several CAR-T-cell therapies targeting these antigens have entered early-phase clinical trials in EBV-associated malignancies (e.g., NCT05864924, NCT04657965, NCT02980315, and NCT05587543), providing translatable evidence for chronic EBV infection [142–145]. These studies assess antigen accessibility within solid tissues, CAR-T-cell expansion and persistence, and the safety and clearance efficiency of target cells. The resulting safety and efficacy data will form the basis for translation into chronic infection. Notably, NCT05864924 has completed phase I and progressed to phase II, demonstrating favorable safety and, in the high-dose cohort, significant antitumor and antiviral activity with reductions in peripheral EBV DNA [142]. This trial provides some of the strongest support for the clinical translation of EBV-CAR-T cells.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: From the validation of CAR-T efficacy in chronic viral infections using animal and in vitro models to its eventual clinical application in humans, multiple barriers remain. First, the safety threshold is quite high and requires stringent control of CAR-T-associated risks in human subjects. Second, challenges in product manufacturing have arisen, as novel clinical contexts impose new technical requirements. Lastly, clinical trial design and ethical considerations add further complexity. Collectively, these barriers have significantly delayed the transition from model validation to standardized clinical application.

sec.title: Clinical complications and adverse reactions
sec.p: Despite its promise, CAR-T-cell therapy has well-known risks, and potential multiorgan toxicity represents a significant limitation for its use in treating chronic viral infections [146]. However, published human studies of CAR-T-cell therapy for chronic viral infections have demonstrated good tolerability. Notably, they did not report significant cytokine release syndrome (CRS), hematologic toxicity, or hypogammaglobulinemia—complications commonly associated with CD19-directed CAR-T-cell therapy [25]. Based on these findings, it can be hypothesized that virus-targeted CAR-T-cell therapy may have a more favorable safety profile than tumor-targeted CAR-T-cell therapy does. Several potential mechanisms may underlie this difference:

Preconditioning Intensity: Cancer patients typically undergo intensive lymphodepletion or myeloablative regimens prior to CAR-T-cell infusion to promote expansion. While effective, such regimens also drive inflammatory cytokine release and robust CAR-T-cell proliferation. In contrast, patients with chronic viral infections often receive no or only minimal lymphodepletion in CAR-T trials (NCT04648046), which may mitigate the risk of cytokine storm-related toxicity.

Lower Viral Burden: Under antiretroviral therapy, most patients present with relatively low viral loads, whereas tumor patients often have a substantial tumor burden. Consequently, CAR-T-cell activation, expansion, and cytotoxic responses are likely to be milder in viral infections, resulting in improved safety [147].
Conservative CAR-T-Cell Dosing: Clinical trials of virus-specific CAR-T-cell therapies typically employ lower and more cautious dosing regimens than those used in cancer treatments [6].

Target Specificity: In oncology, many CAR-T-cell targets are also expressed on normal cells, leading to on-target/off-tumor effects. For example, CD19-CAR-T cells eliminate normal B cells and induce hypogammaglobulinemia. In contrast, CAR-T-cell constructs for viral infections are designed from the outset to avoid human cell surface antigens; instead, virus-specific epitopes are selected, thereby reducing collateral toxicity.

sec.title: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)
sec.p: ICANS can manifest as symptoms ranging from headache and confusion to seizures and even acute cerebral edema. Approximately 43% of CAR-T-cell recipients experience some neurological symptoms, typically with a median onset of approximately 7 days after infusion and a duration of approximately 6 days. Severe cases can progress to coma or death [148]. The risk of ICANS is significantly greater in patients with primary central nervous system (CNS) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated with CAR-T cells, suggesting that the presence of CAR-T target cells in the CNS may be predisposed to neurotoxicity [149]. Notably, approximately 23.9% of CAEBV patients have CNS involvement. In addition, EBV can cause diverse CNS pathologies—including encephalitis, meningitis, demyelination, and EBV-associated lymphoproliferation [150]. Imaging-based and systematic reviews confirm the complexity and breadth of CNS involvement [151]. This result highlights the need for vigilance regarding ICANS risk in patients receiving EBV-CAR-T-cell therapy. Additionally, HIV can establish latent infection in the CNS, particularly in astrocytes, microglia, and perivascular macrophages [152]. In nonhuman primate models, hematopoietic stem cell-derived CD4-CAR-T cells were shown to be engrafted long term and trafficked into multiple CNS compartments [153]. Although no overt clinical toxicity was observed during follow-up, the potential for CAR-T-induced CNS inflammation and ICANS in HIV patients cannot be excluded. Overall, systematic data on the incidence of CAR-T-cell-related neurotoxicity in the context of chronic viral infections remain scarce, indicating an urgent evidence gap that warrants future investigation.

sec.title: On-target organ toxicities
sec.p: Upon antigen recognition, CAR-T cells not only eliminate antigen-bearing cells but also trigger massive cytokine release and activate bystander immune cells such as macrophages, leading to immunopathological damage to target organs [154].

sec.title: Hepatotoxicity
sec.p: Systematic reviews have indicated that approximately 38% of CAR-T-cell-treated patients develop some degree of liver dysfunction, including significant transaminase elevation and cholestasis [155]. HBV-directed CAR-T cells accumulate in the liver and induce robust intrahepatic immune responses [156]. Moreover, patients with chronic HBV frequently present with fibrosis or subclinical impairment of hepatic functional reserve, significantly lowering their tolerance to inflammatory insults [157]. This change predisposes them to CAR-T-induced liver injury. In HBV-CAR-T studies, transient liver function abnormalities have been reported across multiple targets [16, 81, 83]. EBV infection in the context of CAEBV can cause hepatitis, liver dysfunction, and intrahepatic lymphoid aggregation [158–161]. CAR-T-cell-mediated elimination of EBV-infected hepatic tissue could therefore aggravate liver dysfunction.

sec.title: Immunosuppression
sec.p: Latent HIV reservoirs persist in macrophages and lymphocytes [162]. The clearance of these host cells by CAR-T-cell therapy may compromise immune competence. Similarly, EBV persists and proliferates within lymphoid tissues, in which CAR-T-mediated killing or inflammatory disruption can damage the lymphoid architecture and weaken overall immune function [158].

sec.title: Viral escape mutations
sec.p: Because viruses such as HIV and HBV exhibit high genetic variability, CAR-T cells may lose efficacy because viral mutations alter targeted epitopes. In fact, in HIV-related CAR-T clinical trials, researchers have already detected epitope mutations that undermine the persistence of viral control following the infusion of a single CAR-T-cell product [6].

sec.title: CRS
sec.p: The massive expansion and activation of CAR-T cells in vivo can release large quantities of inflammatory cytokines, triggering CRS characterized by high fever, hypotension, and capillary leakage. Between 54% and 91% of anti-tumor CAR-T-cell-treated patients experience some degree of CRS, and severe CRS can lead to respiratory failure, circulatory collapse, and liver or kidney injury [163, 164]. However, in chronic viral infections, owing to lower viral loads and the use of conservative CAR-T-cell dosing, cytokine release tends to be milder, and the observed risk of CRS is relatively low.

sec.title: Cardiotoxicity
sec.p: Meta-analyses report a high incidence of cardiovascular events following CAR-T-cell therapy. Electrocardiographic changes (e.g., ST-segment elevation, arrhythmias) and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction have also been observed relatively frequently [165, 166]. Possibly because of the small sample size, cardiotoxicity has not yet been observed in patients receiving CAR-T-cell therapy for chronic viral infections. Additional evidence is needed in the future.

sec.title: Pulmonary toxicity
sec.p: Although less common, cases of acute interstitial lung disease have been reported in patients after CAR-T-cell therapy [167, 168].

sec.title: Quality of starting T cells
sec.p: In patients with chronic infections, T cells frequently display exhaustion, functional impairment, and phenotypic abnormalities [147]. These features may compromise ex vivo expansion and reduce transduction efficiency. However, similar challenges are also encountered in oncology settings and can be managed by implementing stringent quality control testing prior to product release.

sec.title: Risk of virus-carrying starting T cells
sec.p: T cells may harbor latent viruses such as HIV or EBV, and activation during ex vivo culture can potentially trigger viral reactivation, thereby altering cellular safety [169]. Consequently, virological assessment prior to manufacturing is essential to ensure the selection of virus-free T cells.

sec.title: Interactions between antiretroviral therapy and transduction processes
sec.p: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors commonly used to treat HIV and HBV may interfere with lentiviral vector-based gene transduction [170–172]. Manufacturing SOPs must therefore account for potential drug residues by incorporating appropriate washing steps, drug replacement, or optimized culture conditions.

sec.title: Ethical challenges
sec.p: Risk of Secondary Transmission: In HIV functional cure trials involving analytical treatment interruption (ATI), participants may remain infectious during periods when the viral load is not fully suppressed, posing potential risks to sexual partners or others [173].
Informed Consent: Many patients may lack specialized biomedical knowledge, making it difficult for them to understand the principles, risks, and potential benefits of gene therapy fully [174].

Uncertainty of Long-Term Safety: Gene or vector integration has the possibility of unpredictable, delayed adverse effects [175]. These effects include risks such as insertional mutagenesis leading to oncogenesis or autoimmune and other chronic disorders induced by prolonged immune activation. Such concerns are particularly relevant for therapies involving integrating vectors or novel technologies such as gene editing and CRISPR.

Stigma, Privacy, and Discrimination: Disclosure of infection status or the decision to participate in genetically modified cell therapy could subject participants to societal prejudice and discrimination.

sec.title: Regulatory challenges
sec.p: In the field of gene therapy, regulatory frameworks often mandate up to 15 years of long-term follow-up for therapies using integrating vectors, along with post-marketing surveillance obligations, which introduce significant operational and compliance burdens [176]. Trial design regulation further increases complexity, as ethics and regulatory committees impose strict standards on secondary transmission risks, monitoring schedules, and criteria for treatment re-initiation [177]. In addition, potency assessment and comparability evidence remain as bottlenecks, since standardized frameworks for evaluating antiviral CAR-T-cell function are lacking, and batch-to-batch consistency across multicenter production is difficult to demonstrate [178]. Lastly, environmental and biosafety oversight demands rigorous monitoring of vector shedding and replication-competent vector risks throughout manufacturing and handling [179].

sec.title: Specific research gaps and the responses in this review
Complication Risks
sec.p: Current studies often fail to connect viral organ tropism with downstream complications in a closed-loop framework. In this review, we explicitly align complications such as ICANS, hepatotoxicity, and immunosuppression with strategies to improve safety.

sec.title: Mechanistic synthesis of HBV-CAR-T limitations
sec.p: The literature on HBV cell therapy has focused more on the TCR-T approach than on the CAR-T approach, and few reviews have systematically discussed the reasons behind the slower progress of HBV-CAR-T cells. Here, we dissect major barriers: the “antigen sink” effect, the incomplete presentation of integrated HBV DNA and incomplete cccDNA clearance. Furthermore, we summarize recent preclinical evidence supporting PreS1 as a feasible “bypass” target, thereby outlining a mechanistically informed roadmap for HBV-CAR-T development.

sec.title: Evidence of CMV-CAR-T cells and EBV-CAR-T cells
sec.p: Existing reviews often provide limited coverage of CMV gH-directed CAR-T studies and clinical cases of EBV gp350-CAR-T cells. In response, this review consolidates evidence across the translational continuum—from in vitro assays and animal models to clinical case reports and GMP manufacturing. We discuss both the therapeutic potential and the remaining obstacles, including viral immune evasion and resistance to cytotoxicity mediated by anti-apoptotic proteins.

sec.p: We have reviewed the CAR-T strategies developed for different viral infections (Fig. 2). Future optimization approaches are outlined in Fig. 3, which illustrates several potential directions for improvement, including the following:

sec.title: CAR structure optimization and multifunctional CAR-T
sec.p: CAR design can be enhanced by incorporating features of third- or fourth-generation CARs. For example, multiple co-stimulatory domains can be included. In addition, CAR-T cells can be “armored” to secrete supportive cytokines (such as interleukin 15 (IL-15)). These cytokines create a microenvironment conducive to CAR-T-cell activation and proliferation but may increase the risk of inducing more severe CRS [180, 181]. In addition, CCR5-knockout CAR-T cells can resist HIV infection. However, this design may impair chemotaxis and introduce risks of off-target effects. Additionally, selecting hinge/spacer regions of appropriate length on the basis of the target antigen’s characteristics is crucial to ensuring effective CAR binding and immune synapse formation [182].

sec.title: Stem cell-derived CAR-T cells
sec.p: To overcome the gradual loss of CAR-T-cell populations in patients, researchers are turning to hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Genetically modifying HSCs to express a CAR allows continuous in vivo production of CAR-expressing effector T cells [183]. Notably, HSC-derived CAR-T cells have demonstrated superior persistence and tissue-trafficking capabilities [184].

sec.title: Combination with other Immunotherapies for synergistic effects
sec.p: Single-agent therapy may be insufficient for the complete eradication of chronic infections; thus, combining CAR-T cells with other immunotherapeutic approaches is a promising strategy. For example:

Combining CAR-T cells with virus-specific TCR-T cells: TCR-T cells can target intracellular antigens, complementing CAR-T recognition of surface antigens. This combination reduces immune escape through single viral pathways and provides complementary activation via distinct signaling cascades, ultimately enhancing overall clearance efficiency [185].

Combining CAR-T cells with immune checkpoint inhibitors: Sustained antigen stimulation induces PD-1/PD-L1–mediated CAR-T-cell exhaustion, whereas the checkpoint blockade can restore CAR-T-cell function and prolong CAR-T-cell persistence in vivo, thereby increasing therapeutic efficacy [186, 187].

Therapeutic vaccines: By supplying matched antigens or bridging ligands in vivo, therapeutic vaccines can restimulate and expand infused CAR-T cells, increasing their persistence and effector peak [111]. Therefore, therapeutic vaccines may address the issues of limited CAR-T-cell persistence and the difficulties associated with repeated dosing [188].

Cytokine therapy: Providing low-dose cytokines alongside CAR-T cells may support their proliferation and long-term survival [189]. IL-15 promotes CAR-T-cell proliferation, persistence, and in vivo activity [190]. IL-21 contributes to the generation of TSCM/TCM phenotypes, optimizes oxidative metabolism, and mitigates epigenetic exhaustion [191].

sec.title: Bispecific/Multispecific CAR-T designs
sec.p: CAR-T cells targeting two or more antigens hold promise for improving efficacy and preventing immune escape [192]. This potential can be achieved by co-expressing two distinct CARs in the same T-cell or by linking two different scFvs in tandem within a single CAR structure. These designs enhance their recognition ability and binding strength to infected cells, thereby increasing their killing efficiency [107]. Moreover, this strategy can enable CAR-T cells to combat tumors while also preventing viral reactivation in patients [137, 193].

sec.title: Personalized antiviral CAR-T cells
sec.p: Conventional CAR-T cells can recognize only a limited set of fixed antigenic epitopes, making them vulnerable to viral mutations that lead to immune escape and therapeutic failure. This limitation highlights the need to develop personalized antiviral CAR-T-cell strategies.

One approach involves the generation of TCR-like CAR-T cells that recognize HLA-presented viral peptides [194, 195]. Another approach involves constructing a “universal CAR backbone + interchangeable antibody” platform, in which replacing the antibody component could rapidly redirect CAR-T cells toward different viral epitopes [196]. Large-scale in vitro antibody fragment libraries and single-cell BCR sequencing can generate high-affinity candidate antibody pools in a high-throughput manner, from which patients can be matched to obtain personalized CARs and CAR-T therapies [197, 198].

sec.title: Strategies to improve CAR-T safety
sec.p: Reversible pharmacological switches: Researchers have reported that the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib can reversibly suppress CAR-T-cell cytotoxicity, cellular activation, and cytokine release [199]. Clinically, this strategy enables the rapid attenuation of toxicity once it emerges. Compared with earlier approaches employing suicide genes, the major advantage of this approach is that CAR-T-cell activity can be restored after drug withdrawal, thereby balancing safety with therapeutic efficacy.

Local delivery strategy: Traditionally, CAR-T cells are administered systemically via intravenous infusion. Researchers are now exploring the local delivery of CAR-T cells directly into disease sites to minimize their distribution to off-target organs and thereby reduce systemic toxicity [200]. This strategy holds particular promise for preventing central nervous system toxicity in the treatment of CMV and HIV.

Orthogonal Cytokine-Receptor Pairs: The orthogonal cytokine-receptor system consists of an engineered IL-2 ligand (oIL-2) and its cognate receptor. oIL-2 specifically activates the engineered receptor but not the native IL-2 pathway. Thus, CAR-T-cell activation becomes controllable while systemic IL-2 toxicity is minimized. Both in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that CAR-T cells engineered with orthogonal cytokine-receptor pairs show reduced nonspecific immune activation and diminished IL-2-related side effects [201, 202].

sec.title: Ethics and regulation
sec.p: Ethical safeguards in CAR-T-cell clinical trials for chronic viral infections require enhanced informed consent with clear communication of objectives, risks, and uncertain benefits as well as mechanisms to assess participant comprehension [203]. Protocols must also ensure risk reduction of secondary transmission through protective measures, close monitoring during treatment interruption, and rapid therapy reinitiation pathways [173]. Long-term follow-up is essential to detecting and managing delayed adverse effects, while privacy protection and anti-discrimination safeguards should be embedded in data sharing and reporting processes. Lastly, rigorous biosafety oversight—including validated vector systems, shedding and RCL/RCR testing, environmental release assessments, and emergency protocols—remains indispensable [204].

sec.title: Future potential impact
sec.p: In addition to viral infection, CAR-T-cell therapy has potential for extrapolation to other chronic infectious diseases. Preclinical evidence has already demonstrated the efficacy of CAR-T-cell therapy in fungal infection models, and pathogen-derived epitopes from fungi (e.g., cell wall polysaccharides) have been validated as targets [205–208]. These findings provide a foundation for future clinical translation.

If CAR-T-cell therapy is successful in treating chronic viral infections, its impact on global health could be extensive. In immunocompromised patients, such as transplant recipients, effective control of CMV or EBV reactivation markedly improves prognosis and quality of life. For patients with drug resistance, CAR-T-cell therapy is a novel modality that bypasses resistance mechanisms and restores efficacy. Moreover, by precisely targeting viral reservoirs in HIV and HBV, CAR-T-cell therapy has the potential to achieve a “functional cure” without lifelong medication. This development would represent a breakthrough for hundreds of millions of affected individuals worldwide. Lastly, success in this domain could lead to the establishment of CAR-T-cell therapy as a model for other chronic diseases, including autoimmune and fibrotic disorders, heralding a new era in precision cellular medicine.

Despite of the considerable promise, the journey of the CAR-T-cell therapy to routine clinical use across chronic viral infections is likely to be long. Given its rapid progress, the clinical approval for an HIV-directed CAR-T therapy might emerge within the next decade. However, the wide, routine use of the CAR-T-cell therapy will likely lag by several years, requiring post-approval validation, manufacturing scale-up, and accrual of clinical experience.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Despite many attempts to develop a cure, chronic viral infections have remained a major public health issue. Current treatments for these diseases, in addition to their side effects, are unable to eradicate the virus and prevent reactivation. Therefore, finding a cure that eliminates the virus is necessary. Mounting evidence has indicated that CAR-T-cell therapy holds significant promise against viruses such as HIV, HBV, CMV, and EBV. In the context of these viral infections, CAR-T cells can specifically recognize and eliminate virus-infected cells. However, translating this approach to widespread clinical use still faces major hurdles, including the biological difficulty of eradicating chronic viruses, the need for further validation of clinical safety, the technical challenges of consistent product manufacture, and the complex ethical and regulatory requirements. At present, multiple CAR-T designs have been developed. The most promising future direction for CAR-T therapy in chronic viral infections may lie in the combination of HSC/iPSC-derived CAR-T cells and bispecific CARs. Stem cell-derived CAR-T cells provide the essential temporal dimension. In addition, bispecific CARs can markedly reduce antigen escape and maintain cytotoxicity under conditions of repeated or alternating antigen exposure. Together, this combination defines a paradigm-shifting roadmap for the next generation of CAR-T-cell therapies in chronic viral infections.
